701.quote_or_event: “He alone is a Sikh, a friend, a relative and a sibling, who walks in the Way of the Guru's Will.”
701.explanation: Guru Amar Das defines the true disciple as one who lives inside the Guru's bhana (will), already moving with it rather than waiting to be told.
701.tie_back: The Kural praises the one who grasps a master's intention without a word being said; Gurbani honours the Sikh who is so attuned that he walks within the Guru's will.
701.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 601, Raag Sorath, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
701._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the verse is about spiritual surrender to the Guru's will, not a courtier's skill at reading a ruler's face.

702.quote_or_event: “You are permeating each and every heart, O Lord, Inner-knower, Searcher of Hearts.”
702.explanation: Antarjami, the Inner-knower who sees what lies within every heart, is one of Gurbani's most frequent names for God.
702.tie_back: The Kural calls the one who perceives another's mind without doubt equal to a god; in Gurbani, knowing the heart from within is precisely the mark of the divine.
702.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 96, Raag Maajh, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
702._accuracy_note: A real echo of heart-reading as god-like, but Gurbani reserves this knowledge to God and does not credit perceptive humans with it.

703.quote_or_event: “Surrender body, mind, wealth, and everything to the Guru; obey the Order of His Will, and you will find Him.”
703.explanation: In Anand Sahib, Guru Amar Das tells the seeker to hand over body, mind and wealth to the Guru, who knows the inner state, and to live by his hukam.
703.tie_back: The Kural says those who read inner intentions should be won whatever part of one's wealth it costs; Anand Sahib says to give everything to the Guru who sees within.
703.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 918, Raag Ramkali, Anand Sahib, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
703._accuracy_note: Next-best: both speak of paying any price to gain one who knows the heart, but the Kural means recruiting perceptive advisers, while Anand Sahib means spiritual surrender.

704.quote_or_event: Sikh tradition tells how a jug fell into mud and Guru Nanak asked his sons to pick it up; they refused the dirty, menial task, but Bhai Lehna lifted it out, washed it clean and brought it back full of water. Guru Nanak later named Lehna, renamed Angad, as his successor instead of his own sons.
704.explanation: The sons and the disciple stood equally close to the Guru, yet only Lehna understood and carried out what the Guru wanted; the story is one of several told to explain his choice as Guru Angad.
704.tie_back: The Kural says those who grasp a master's intent unbidden and those who do not may look alike in body yet are different kinds of people; the Guru's sons and Lehna show exactly this.
704.source: Wikipedia, 'Guru Angad' (summarising W. Owen Cole and Piara Singh Sambhi, The Sikhs: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices, 1978, p. 18)
704._accuracy_note: A strong thematic fit, but this is hagiographic tradition, checked only through Wikipedia's summary of Cole and Sambhi because Macauliffe's text on sacred-texts.com would not load; the story stresses humble obedience as much as perception.

705.quote_or_event: “Do not call them blind, who have no eyes in their face. They alone are blind, O Nanak, who wander away from their Lord and Master.”
705.explanation: Guru Angad redefines blindness: having eyes in the face counts for nothing if they do not see what truly matters.
705.tie_back: The Kural asks what use the eyes are among the body's organs if they cannot read intention; Guru Angad likewise says eyes that do not perceive leave a person blind.
705.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 954, Raag Ramkali, Ramkali ki Vaar (salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
705._accuracy_note: Strong on the rhetoric that seeing eyes without perception are worthless; Gurbani's perception is of the Lord, while the Kural's is of another person's intent.

706.quote_or_event: “Those who have meditated on the Naam, the Name of the Lord, and departed after having worked by the sweat of their brows -O Nanak, their faces are radiant in the Court of the Lord, and many are saved along with them!”
706.explanation: The closing salok of Japji Sahib says that the inner labour of remembering the Name shows outwardly as a radiant face.
706.tie_back: The Kural says the face shows whatever is strongest in the heart, as crystal shows its neighbour's colour; Japji says the devotion within becomes visible as radiance on the face.
706.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8, Japji Sahib (closing salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
706._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: 'radiant face' in Gurbani is also an idiom for honour before God, and there is no crystal image or general claim about faces mirroring every feeling.

707.quote_or_event: “One who meditates on the Naam is at peace; his face is radiant and bright.” … “The faithless cynic barks out his lies, and his face is blackened.”
707.explanation: In two hymns Guru Arjan describes the inner state showing on the face: the peace of the Name brightens it, while falsehood darkens it.
707.tie_back: The Kural says the face is the first to announce whether a person is pleased or angry; Guru Arjan likewise treats the face as the place where the inner condition becomes visible.
707.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 44, Sri Raag, Guru Arjan; and Ang 239, Raag Gauri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
707._accuracy_note: Next-best: Gurbani's bright and blackened faces are partly idioms for honour and disgrace, and it does not speak of pleasure or anger registering on the face first.

708.quote_or_event: “You know completely the condition of my mind; who else could I go to tell of it?”
708.explanation: Guru Arjan tells God that the whole condition (birtha) of his mind is already known to Him, so there is no need to explain it to anyone.
708.tie_back: The Kural says that before those who look into the heart it is enough simply to stand and be seen; Guru Arjan says the Lord already knows the mind's trouble without being told.
708.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 382, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
708._accuracy_note: A strong fit on not needing to speak before one who knows the heart; the knower here is God, not a perceptive minister or friend.

709.quote_or_event: “Bronze is bright and shiny, but when it is rubbed, its blackness appears.”
709.explanation: According to the Janamsakhi tradition, Guru Nanak sang this hymn to Sajjan, a welcoming host who secretly robbed and killed travellers; the shining surface hid an inner blackness, and Sajjan repented.
709.tie_back: The Kural says those who understand glances can tell an enemy from a friend; Guru Nanak saw the enemy beneath Sajjan's friendly surface.
709.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Suhi, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
709._accuracy_note: Partial: the Sajjan story is Janamsakhi hagiography, and the verse warns that outward shine can deceive rather than trusting the eye to reveal enmity as the Kural does.

710.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, those eyes are different, which behold my Husband Lord.”
710.explanation: Guru Arjan says that truly seeing eyes are of another kind altogether: the eyes that see the Beloved.
710.tie_back: The Kural says the only measuring rod of the truly discerning is the eye; Gurbani also makes the quality of one's seeing the real measure, though of the divine rather than of other people.
710.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 577, Raag Vadhans, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
710._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the verse uses bride-soul imagery for spiritual, not romantic, sight of God and says nothing about using the eye to judge others.
